questions.question: A solid cuboid is built out of centimetre cubes. Its bottom layer is a rectangle of cubes 4 cubes long and 3 cubes wide, so one full layer uses 12 cubes. The cuboid is 5 layers tall, and every layer is full. What is the volume of the cuboid?
options: 60 cm³
94 cm³
17 cm³
12 cm³
questions.explain: Volume of a right prism is base area × height, so one layer of 12 cubes repeated 5 times gives 12 × 5 = 60 cm³. The trap is answering 94, which is the area of the outside faces (surface area), not the number of cubes inside.

questions.question: A solid cuboid is made of 1 cm cubes. Its bottom layer is completely covered by 20 cubes, and the cuboid is 3 layers tall with every layer full, so its volume is 20 × 3 = 60 cm³. Which statement best explains WHY you multiply 20 by 3?
options: The 20 cubes cover the outside of the solid, and multiplying by 3 counts each outside face once.
Every layer is an exact copy of the base, so the 20 cubes of the base area are repeated once for each of the 3 centimetres of height.
20 is the length of the cuboid and 3 is its width, so multiplying them gives the whole solid.
A cuboid always has 3 pairs of faces, so the base area is multiplied by 3.
questions.explain: Height tells you how many copies of the base are stacked, which is why volume = base area × height for any right prism. The common trap is thinking the base area describes the outside covering of the solid; that idea belongs to surface area, not volume.

questions.question: A solid cuboid has a bottom face measuring 6 cm by 5 cm, and it stands 4 cm tall. Which calculation gives its volume?
questions.explain: First find the base area, 6 × 5 = 30 cm², then multiply by the height: 30 × 4 = 120 cm³. The trap is the long sum of all six faces — that is surface area, which measures covering, not filling.

questions.question: A solid cuboid has a base whose area is 20 cm², and the cuboid is 6 cm tall. What is its volume?
options: 26 cm³
20 cm³
120 cm²
120 cm³
questions.explain: Volume = base area × height = 20 × 6 = 120, and because it measures space filled the unit is cm³. Watch the unit trap: the same number written as 120 cm² would be an area, and area cannot describe how much fits inside.

questions.question: A chocolate bar is a right triangular prism. Its triangular end face has an area of 14 cm², and the bar is 9 cm long from one end face to the other. What is the volume of the bar?
options: 126 cm³
28 cm³
23 cm³
63 cm³
questions.explain: For any right prism, volume = base area × height, and here the triangular end is the base, so 14 × 9 = 126 cm³. A common trap is doubling the end face to get 28, which only adds the two triangular faces — that is part of the wrapper, not the chocolate.

questions.question: A cylindrical juice can from a Vancouver corner store has a circular base with an area of 50 cm², and the can is 12 cm tall. About how much juice fits inside?
options: 62 cm³
600 cm³
300 cm³
100 cm²
questions.explain: A cylinder works like any right prism: base area × height = 50 × 12 = 600 cm³. The trap is answering 100 cm², which is just the two circular ends — metal you can touch, not juice you can pour.

questions.question: Two right prisms are both 8 cm tall. Prism A has a rectangular base with area 30 cm². Prism B has a hexagonal base with area 30 cm². Which statement is true?
options: Prism A holds more, because only a rectangular prism can be found with length × width × height.
Prism B holds more, because a hexagon has more sides, so the prism has more faces to fill.
Their volumes are equal, because each one is 30 × 8 = 240 cm³.
You cannot compare them without knowing the side lengths of each base.
questions.explain: Volume = base area × height works for every right prism, so equal base areas and equal heights mean equal volumes, no matter what shape the base is. The trap is counting faces or sides — that describes the surface, which has nothing to do with how much fits inside.

questions.question: A right prism has base area B and height h. A second right prism has exactly the same base, but it is twice as tall. How do the volumes compare?
options: The volume stays the same, because the base area did not change.
The volume is 4 × B × h, because both the base and the height are involved.
You cannot tell, because making the prism taller also changes its surface area.
The volume is 2 × B × h, because doubling the height stacks twice as many copies of the base.
questions.explain: Height counts how many copies of the base are stacked, so twice the height means twice the volume: B × 2h = 2Bh. A frequent trap is worrying about the changed surface area — surface area and volume are different measurements, and volume only needs base area × height.

questions.question: Maya is figuring out how much soil fills a closed planter box shaped like a right rectangular prism, 4 m long, 3 m wide and 2 m high. She writes 52 and says that is the volume. What happened, and what is the correct volume?
options: She added the areas of the six faces, which is surface area; the volume is (4 × 3) × 2 = 24 m³.
She forgot to double her answer, so the volume is 104 m³.
She should have added 4 + 3 + 2 first, so the volume is 9 m³.
She is correct: 52 counts every face of the box, and that is what volume means.
questions.explain: Volume fills the box: base area 4 × 3 = 12 m², times height 2 m, gives 24 m³. Maya's 52 comes from 2(12) + 2(8) + 2(6), the total of the six faces — that is the cardboard around the box, measured in m², not the soil inside.

questions.question: A cylindrical rain barrel in a Surrey community garden has a base area of 1 800 cm². After a dry week the water stands 40 cm deep. A rainstorm raises the water level to 55 cm. How much water did the storm add to the barrel?
options: 1 815 cm³
questions.explain: The water added is its own prism of water: the base area stays 1 800 cm², and the height that was added is 55 − 40 = 15 cm, so 1 800 × 15 = 27 000 cm³. The usual trap is multiplying by the final depth of 55 cm, which gives all the water in the barrel instead of just the new rain.

questions.question: At a school movie night there are two popcorn containers, both 10 cm tall. The box is a right rectangular prism with a base measuring 20 cm by 15 cm. The tub is a cylinder with a circular base of area 300 cm². Which container holds more popcorn?
options: The box, because it has six flat faces to hold popcorn while the tub has only three surfaces.
The box, because 20 × 15 × 10 = 3 000 cm³ is much more than the tub's 300 cm².
They hold the same amount: both bases are 300 cm² and both heights are 10 cm, so both hold 3 000 cm³.
The tub, because a round container always holds more than a box of the same height.
questions.explain: Find each base area first: the box's base is 20 × 15 = 300 cm², the same as the tub's, and with equal heights both give base area × height = 300 × 10 = 3 000 cm³. The trap is comparing faces or comparing a volume in cm³ against a base area in cm² — the tub's 300 cm² still has to be multiplied by its height.

questions.question: A raised garden bed in Kelowna is a right prism. Its base is an L-shape made from a 3 m by 2 m rectangle joined to a 1 m by 2 m rectangle, and the bed is 0.5 m deep everywhere. Soil costs $30 for each cubic metre. What does it cost to fill the bed with soil?
questions.explain: Split the L-shaped base: 3 × 2 = 6 m² and 1 × 2 = 2 m², so the base area is 8 m²; then volume = 8 × 0.5 = 4 m³, and 4 × $30 = $120. The most common trap is paying for 8 — that is an area in m², and soil is sold by the cubic metre, so the depth must still be multiplied in.
